lines.text: This is a reinforcer assessment. A preference assessment told us what the student picks. This tells us whether getting it makes a behavior more likely, which is the only thing a plan can use. The way to find out is to measure a response with the item delivered for it, and without.

The response is chosen first: something the student can already do, easy to count, that produces nothing by itself, and that takes a little effort, so it stops when nothing follows. Here it is placing one block in the bin, counted when the block lands.

The control condition comes first: the same tray, the same bin, the assessor present and neutral. The student places a block now and then, and nothing happens. The session runs five minutes, and the measure is responses per minute. This is the rate the stimulus has to beat.

Now the tablet condition. Every block in the bin produces the tablet, within two seconds, for twenty seconds, the same way every time. The session clock pauses during the access, so the rate is responses per minute of available time. Then the tablet goes away, and the next block earns the next access.

Watch the counter. The rate climbs, and it stays up across sessions, while control stays low. That difference, replicated, is the reinforcement effect: not that the student likes the tablet, but that the tablet changes what the student does.

Each session is one row on the sheet, and the graph plots the conditions side by side. The verdict is read from the ratio to control and the overlap: twice the control rate, no overlap, at least three sessions of each, is a clear effect. The numbers support the visual analysis; they do not replace it.

Praise with a high five was chosen almost half the time in the preference assessment. Under the single-operant test its rate sits with control. Preferred is not the same as reinforcing. That is why we test.

Concurrent operants ask a different question: which one, when both are there for the same work. Two identical bins, the same distance away. A block in one earns the tablet, a block in the other earns the fruit chew, and a third bin produces nothing. The positions rotate across sessions, so a side bias shows up as a side bias.
The student allocates. Most blocks go to the tablet's bin, some to the fruit chew's, almost none to the control. The measure is allocation: each option's share of the responses, session by session.

This is a relative test. The fruit chew's small share does not mean it is not a reinforcer; alone, it was. It means the tablet beats it when both are available, which is what a plan with a choice needs to know.

The progressive-ratio test asks how much work the stimulus will support. The first tablet costs one block, and the requirement grows by a fixed step after every reinforcer. The student keeps working while the tablet is worth it. When no response comes for the stop interval, the session ends, and the break point is the last ratio completed.

Break points are compared across stimuli under the same step, stop interval and cap. A break point well above the plan's schedule says the stimulus can carry it. A break point near the control's says it cannot. One break point is unstable: two or three sessions per stimulus, and a no-reinforcer control.

Three rules hold for every design. Deliver the stimulus immediately, in a fixed magnitude, with no added praise. Keep a no-consequence control with the same materials. Restrict access to the stimulus for a few hours before the session, and record any access there was. Record problem behavior every session, and have a second observer on about one session in three when the result goes into a plan.

At the table, the sheet's runner does the counting. It times the session, cues each delivery and times the access, counts the responses you tap, and writes the row when you save. Space or R for a response, P for problem behavior.

The summary sheet lines the tests up for each stimulus: the preference rank, the single-operant ratio, the concurrent allocation, the break point, and a verdict. The reinforcer of record is the one confirmed by an absolute test. A stimulus that only won the concurrent test is relative only. And the plan's schedule comes from the break point.
